newsitem.title: MEXICO: Union Pacific sees synergies in Mexico rail.
newsitem.headline: Union Pacific sees synergies in Mexico rail.

text.p: Mexico's largest railway offers key synergies with Union Pacific Corp's U.S.-Mexico border connections, Union Pacific director general in Mexico Juan Manuel Carreon said on Monday.
Union Pacific joined with Mexican builder Empresas ICA Sociedad Controladora SA de CV and mining giant Grupo Mexico SA to compose the lone bid in the Pacific-North railway privatization.

"The synergies with the Pacific-North line and Union Pacific's connections are at Piedras Negras, Coahuila; Ciudad Juarez, Chihuahua; Mexicali, Baja California; and Nogales, Sonora," Carreon said in a phone interview, highlighting border connections between Mexico and the United States.

The 6,500-km Pacific-North line is Mexico's largest, and carries about 45 percent of the nation's cargo. Aside from border connections, the railway spans to city centers of Mexico City, Monterrey and Guadalajara and ports Mazatlan, Manzanillo, and Topolobampo.
"We've made inspections and it needs improvements, but in general terms it's in very good shape," Carreon said.

Although the consortium is the only bidder, government privatization coordinator Jorge Silberstein said the group must surpass an undisclosed minimum bid. The technical proposals for the route are scheduled to be opened June 19, economic bids should be opened on June 26 and a decision is expected to be reached by July 7.
Carreon said Grupo Mexico would lead the bid but declined to detail the companies' percentage participation in the consortium or other specific plans for the route.
"The area has a lot of automotive and intermodal potential," he said. "It also has great agricultural possibilities."

Grupo Mexico has eyed the route because of its connections to the company's key copper interests, particularly the route's Chihuahua-Pacific line. Grupo Mexico is easily Mexico's largest copper producer
Last year the Chihuahua-Pacifico line bidding was aborted after Grupo Mexico's lone bid did not meet the government's minimum price for the rail.
An original three bidders for the Pacific-North line shrunk to one, after builder Grupo Tribasa dropped out and Grupo Mexico joined the ICA and Union Pacific venture.
